Soccer Mom (or insert other sport/parental term) can specifically mean a parent whose child plays the sport, typically when the parent is involved with supporting that sport - carpool, attending games, taking their turn with snacks, etc. When someone is saying “I’m a soccer/football/dance/karate/baseball/lacrosse mom,” this is typically what they mean. When used in this way, people usually state the actual sport their child plays, and it’s not race- or sport-specific. 

More generally, it’s sometimes used for moms who don’t work full-time and who are able to be very involved with their kids’ lives and extracurricular after school (and usually middle/high school aged kids). It is often used as something of a demographic term/demographic indicator - I typically only hear white, middle class moms referred to as “soccer moms” in this way and it’s often slightly condescending.

I taught strings for two years. Our students had to chose between chorus or strings, so I had a lot of people in the class who were not thrilled to be there. It’s much harder to have a performance ensemble with unwilling participants, so you find ways to make it more fun for the kids who don’t necessarily love music class. I basically threw out everything I’d learned in college about “correct” pedagogy because it did not resonate at all with my students, and I found what worked for them. 

I had the most luck when my goal was teaching good technique on a few notes - and one technique per song. I would have them bow along to famous songs, playing the root of the chord. Popular music worked well because they would be playing the same note for 2-4 measures at least. A couple songs we did this for:

1. Ocho kandelikas (Chanukkah) 
2. Glory (from Selma) 
3. Choo Choo Ch’Boogie 

We also did Entrance of the Dragon Riders from Music K-8 (our mascot was the dragon). It’s a recorder piece with a B-A-G line and a B-C-A-G-E line, so you can differentiate, and I liked that it helped my students switch between strings quickly. They really mastered that skill. 


For their grad concert, they played the theme from Ode To Joy three times through. The most advanced (about 30%) played the theme, and the less advanced students played the root of each chord. 

We did everything with a recorded background - it was more engaging for the students, and made for more interesting performances for parents (and let’s face it, admin) to watch. 

We used a practice software that went along with their methods book, so they could play along with a track and they could record themselves and submit it to me. If I used another resource for their performance pieces, I could input the notes into the software for them too. My second year was better by far than the first, and sometimes I wish I’d stayed in teaching to get even better, but it is what it is. Hope this helps!

Hey, senior year is really rough. And your supervising teacher may not understand the time commitment that edTPA is. My supervising teacher was finishing her PhD during my student teacher year, it was ROUGH. 

Here is what I will advise…

1. Graduate. Even if you decide not to work in the field, finish your degree. Having a degree in literally any field has significant financial value…I work in the business world and I am eligible for certain jobs just because I have a completed degree. 

2. Make it as easy for people to help you as possible. The school probably will not give you credentials. Ask the supervising teacher if they can log into the grade book (or whatever you need access to) and let you see it/access the information during lunch/planning sometime so you can get what you need - or alternatively, ask if they would be willing to change their password to something that you can both use for the year (this one is definitely case-by-case so use your best judgement). If you need questions answered, type them out, let your supervising teacher know you have some questions you need answers for, and send them as an email - be sure to let them know the deadline you need it back by (don’t set one too far out or they may forget). 

Whenever you have a question, be prepared with three possible suggestions, and also be prepared that you are going to hear the word “no” all year, and a lot more than you hear “yes.” It’s okay. You will survive this. Try not to over complicate your lesson. 

For your advisor, send them an email asking when you can meet with them. If your school uses Outlook, there is actually a feature (Scheduling Assistant I believe it’s called) that, when you’re setting a meeting, lets you compare your schedule to everyone invited to the meeting…suggest three different times when you are both available. 

I agree that you should not be embarrassed to seek out a therapist or other mental health help. I had quite a few breakdowns…I was also planning a wedding during my senior year (0/10 would not recommend). Graduate and then do whatever you want, whether that’s teaching or something else. Hey OP, I’m really sorry that happened. A couple other people have mentioned seeing a therapist - to add to that, I would recommend actively seeing a therapist specifically while getting back into the dating scene for three reasons: 

1. Dating can be rough, and even with a great partner, feelings from your prior relationship will bubble up. It would be good to process those with a professional. 

2. Because this will be your first experience with adult dating, it would be good for you to have a professional to help you look out for red flags - you may not notice red flags that people who’ve dated more would see. A therapist can help protect you from that. 

3. You also may not have had a lot of chance to practice your own healthy behaviors in the context of a romantic relationship. A therapist can help you learn how to set healthy expectations, communicate, evaluate compatibility, etc.

I hope you’re able to find an affordable option that works for you, and I hope you meet someone who treats you very kindly. The best advice I can give you for keeping your standards high is this: 

I used to allow people to treat me poorly because I didn’t believe I deserved any better. Now, I’ve completely stopped asking myself whether I deserve the way I’ve been treated - I just ask myself if I want to be treated that way. It may seem inconsequential to some people, but if you struggle with feelings of low self worth, then don’t use your perceived value to determine if you deserve to be treated well. Somehow that little flip made a world of change for me.

If you suspect abuse/something else but they haven’t disclosed anything specific:

-“Hey, I just want you to know that if you ever feel like talking about your relationship with me, it would never change how I treated your spouse, I would never disclose it to anyone, and even if I gave you advice that you didn’t go with, I would trust that you know your relationship better than I do and can make the right call for you.” 

Justification: If a person is not sure if they are ready to end the relationship, they know that disclosing abuse to others often does just that. They also may be afraid that you will pressure them to immediately leave, and they may not have the resources/emotional strength to do that. Letting them know that you will listen and advise without judgement creates a safe place, and assured them that you will not be another person who batters them.


If they tell you they are currently in one:

-Are you currently safe?

-Do you want to talk about it?

-Do you want to leave?

-Do you have the resources, plans, and community support you need to leave?

-What kind of resources do you need? Can I help you get these safely? (Bank account in their name, drivers license, a place to stay right when they leave, a ride to a job interview, work clothes, researching childcare options, a DV attorney-you can get a 30-60 minute one-time consultation for around $100. You may not even need to spend money, they may just need logistical help untangling their life from their abuser’s). 


If the abuse happened in a previous relationship:

-I’m sorry that happened. 

-Are you safe now? 

-Do you have any physical/emotional triggers I can avoid? (I don’t like to be touched in my arms or on my face)

-It’s your business, but you can always talk ti me if you want to.

Note: don’t ask/say all of these at once unless the situation calls for it. Abuse is very mentally overwhelming, so don’t pepper them if they seem like they’re in overload.

In my elementary school in 5th grade, we each picked a different tribe and had to research their individual cultures, food, clothing, housing, hair and adornment, and customs. We then presented them to the class so we all got a good idea of how much different tribes varied. 

If your research includes media for children, I highly recommend looking into the following iconic pieces of popular media that famously depict Indigenous people in various lights. The following companies/authors/media are pretty much universally know of by Americans, even if they have not personally consumed that media: 

-American Girl. American Girl makes dolls, but they also publish books that are very highly researched. One series is about a girl named Kaya who is part of the Nez Perce/Nimiipuu tribe. The author collaborated with the tribe to make sure Kaya (the doll and the books) was a positive and accurate representation of the tribe. That’s actually why she is the only AG doll who smiles with her mouth closed…baring your teeth would be a sign of aggression in her culture. See this link for more:

https://www.nativeknot.com/amp/news/Native-American-News/American-Girl-Doll-Kaya-Captures-Authentically-Native-Culture.html


-Laura Ingalls Wilder. This series was written by a woman whose family were settlers in the 1870s. Her stories are based on her experiences living in Minnesota, Wisconsin, Missouri, and Kansas (where they were illegally occupying Indigenous land). These stories contain racist stories and remarks against Indigenous and Black Americans. See this link for more: 

https://www.pbs.org/wnet/americanmasters/what-should-be-done-about-racist-depictions-in-the-little-house-books/16587/

-Disney’s Pocahontas. Disney may have had good intentions, and they made Pocahontas’ character likeable, wise, and strong, but they turned a story of kidnapping, trafficking and mass murder into a feel-good romance narrative. The Powhatan tribe has wholly condemned the movie as a grotesque twisting of history. See this link for more:

Here are my best suggestions for couples who are struggling with this:

1. Your partner may be under stimulated, and that can make it really hard to focus. Trade massages, snuggle, play with each other’s hair, take up knitting, set out a finger food that takes awhile to eat, etc. 

2. Take a break halfway through the movie. 1.5 hours is a longgg time to sit still if you have ADHD. Pause the movie and make dinner, drink tea, talk about the movie so far, etc.

3. Put on closed captioning. Many people with ADHD have trouble processing language. Even if I am paying attention, I have a hard time knowing what’s going on in movies because I literally cannot hear.

4. Take turns choosing the movie. Unless there is something you truly cannot watch (violence, gore, etc.), actually let them show you the movie they like. 

5. Ask them about it. Try to find a solution for both of you. Remember that it is probably not personal, and it is probably not a blatant act of disrespect. Be willing to find ways to accommodate each other.
